title: Chemical Reactions and Equations — Chapter Summary
intro: When one substance turns into another — milk into curd, iron into rust, paper into ash — a chemical reaction has happened. Chemistry's job is to recognise these reactions, write them compactly using formulas, balance them so that no atom is created or destroyed, classify them into a few useful types, and use this language to understand and predict change in the everyday world.

sections.heading: Chemical Equations
bullets: Word equation: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide.
Chemical equation: Mg + O₂ → MgO.
Reactants on the LEFT; products on the RIGHT.
Indicators of a reaction: colour change, gas evolution, precipitate, temperature change, state change.
Symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous; ↑ gas, ↓ precipitate; Δ heat needed.

sections.heading: Balancing Equations
bullets: Law of conservation of mass: atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
Balanced equation: same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
Use COEFFICIENTS (numbers in front of formulas) — never change subscripts.
Strategy: balance one element at a time; balance H and O last.
Verify by counting atoms after.

sections.heading: Types of Reactions
bullets: COMBINATION: A + B → AB. Example: 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO.
DECOMPOSITION: AB → A + B. Driven by HEAT (thermal), LIGHT (photochemical) or ELECTRICITY (electrolytic).
DISPLACEMENT: more reactive element displaces less reactive from its compound. Example: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT: AB + CD → AD + CB. Often gives a precipitate. Example: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃.
REDOX: oxidation (gain of O / loss of H) and reduction (loss of O / gain of H) happen TOGETHER.

sections.heading: Energy Changes
bullets: EXOTHERMIC: heat released; surroundings warm up. Example: combustion (CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O + heat).
ENDOTHERMIC: heat absorbed; surroundings cool down. Example: photosynthesis or thermal decomposition of CaCO₃.
Most COMBINATION reactions are exothermic.
Most DECOMPOSITION reactions are endothermic — energy must be supplied to break things apart.
Slaking of lime (CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂) is strongly exothermic — fizzes and gets hot.

sections.heading: Oxidation in Everyday Life — Corrosion and Rancidity
bullets: CORROSION: slow eating-away of metals by air, moisture, chemicals.
Iron rusts: Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (orange-brown).
Copper develops a green coating (basic copper carbonate).
Silver tarnishes black (silver sulphide).
Prevention: paint, oil, galvanise (zinc), tin-plate, alloy (stainless steel).
RANCIDITY: oxidation of oils / fats in food causing bad smell and taste.
Prevention: airtight packaging (sometimes nitrogen-flushed), antioxidants, refrigeration.

key_takeaways: A chemical reaction converts reactants into products; observable indicators help us spot one.
Balanced equations satisfy the law of conservation of mass — atoms are conserved.
Five reaction types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox.
Decomposition can be thermal, photochemical, or electrolytic.
Exothermic = heat out; endothermic = heat in.
Corrosion (rust, tarnish) and rancidity are everyday consequences of oxidation; reducing exposure to oxygen / moisture / light prevents them.

glossary.definition: A process in which one or more substances are transformed into different substances.
A starting substance in a chemical reaction (on the left of the equation).
A substance formed in a chemical reaction (on the right of the equation).
An equation in which the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.
Two or more reactants combine to form a single product (A + B → AB).
A single reactant breaks down into two or more products (AB → A + B).
A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
Two compounds exchange ions (AB + CD → AD + CB), often forming a precipitate.
Gain of oxygen, or loss of hydrogen, by a substance.
Loss of oxygen, or gain of hydrogen, by a substance.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together.
A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings.
A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings.
The slow eating-away of metals by air, moisture and chemicals.
The development of an unpleasant smell and taste in fatty / oily foods due to slow oxidation.
